trials.brief: Write an explanation of about 400 words of what a leap second is and why the bodies that govern timekeeping have decided to stop adding them. The reader is a general newspaper reader.
trials.a:
**The Leap Second, and Why Time's Keepers Are Abandoning It**

A leap second is a one-second adjustment added to the world's clocks, usually at the very end of June or December, so that our timekeeping stays in step with the spinning Earth.

The trouble starts with the fact that there are two ways to measure time. For most of history, we judged time by the planet itself: one rotation made a day, and a day was divided into 86,400 seconds. But Earth is an imperfect clock. Tides drag on its rotation, earthquakes and shifting ice nudge it, and its speed varies unpredictably. Over the long run, days are getting slightly longer.

Since the 1960s there has been a far steadier alternative: atomic clocks, which count the vibrations of atoms and lose almost nothing over millions of years. The second is now defined by those vibrations, not by the Earth's turning. Atomic time and Earth time therefore drift apart. To keep the two within 0.9 seconds of each other, international timekeepers began inserting leap seconds in 1972. Twenty-seven have been added since, the most recent at the end of 2016. On those occasions, clocks briefly read 23:59:60 before rolling over to midnight.

For ordinary people, this barely mattered. For computers, it has been a recurring headache. Software generally assumes every minute has exactly 60 seconds and that time only moves forward. A minute with 61 seconds can confuse systems that do not expect it. Leap seconds have been blamed for crashes and outages at major websites and in networks, and engineers at large technology companies have invented workarounds, such as "smearing" the extra second across a whole day. Because leap seconds cannot be predicted far ahead, being announced only months in advance, systems that depend on precise timing, from financial trading to satellite navigation and power grids, must keep updating their rules.

In 2022, the General Conference on Weights and Measures, the international body that oversees the definition of the second, voted to stop using leap seconds by or before 2035. The plan is to let the gap between atomic time and Earth time grow beyond one second, and to revisit the matter in the future with a new method of correction, perhaps a larger, rarer adjustment of a minute or more.

A surprising development has also helped the case. Earth's rotation has recently been speeding up slightly, which could even call for a "negative" leap second, removing one. That has never been tried, and software engineers dread it more than the usual addition.

In practical terms, the change will be invisible. Noon will remain near the Sun's highest point for generations. The decision simply trades a small, regular fix for a simpler, steadier clock.
trials.b:
A leap second is a one-second adjustment occasionally added to the world's official clocks so that they stay in step with the turning of the Earth. The reason it exists is that there are two ways of measuring time, and they do not quite agree. Atomic clocks count seconds with extraordinary steadiness, using the vibrations of atoms, and they would keep perfect time for millions of years. The Earth, by contrast, is a rather unreliable timekeeper. Its spin is slowed gradually by the pull of the Moon's tides, and it also speeds up and slows down in small, unpredictable ways because of earthquakes, shifting ice, ocean currents and movements in its molten core.

Since 1972, the international standard known as Coordinated Universal Time has tried to serve both masters. It ticks at the pace of atomic clocks, but whenever it drifts too far from the time measured by the planet's rotation, the authorities insert an extra second, usually at the end of June or December. On those occasions a clock goes from 23:59:59 to 23:59:60 before rolling over to midnight. Twenty-seven of these seconds have been added so far, the most recent at the end of 2016.

The trouble is that the modern world runs on computers, and computers dislike a minute with sixty-one seconds. Software generally assumes that every minute has exactly sixty, so a leap second can cause systems to freeze, crash or record events out of order. Several well-known outages have been blamed on leap seconds, affecting websites, airline systems and data centres. Large technology companies developed their own workarounds, such as spreading the extra second across the whole day, but because they did not all do it the same way, the fixes themselves created confusion. Financial markets, telecommunications networks, satellite navigation and power grids all depend on clocks that agree to tiny fractions of a second, and an irregular, unannounced insertion is a risk to each of them.

There is also a quirk in how the Earth has recently behaved. Over the past few years it has been spinning slightly faster than expected, which raises the prospect of a negative leap second, in which a second would be removed. That has never been tried, and engineers fear it would be even more disruptive than adding one.

For these reasons, the international body that sets the measurement standards voted in 2022 to stop using leap seconds by or before 2035. After that date the gap between atomic time and the planet's rotation will be allowed to grow to a minute or so before any correction is considered, probably not for a century or more. For ordinary people, nothing will change in daily life. The Sun will still rise on schedule, and the difference will be far too small to notice.

trials.brief: Write a technical description of about 400 words of how a lithium-ion cell is charged and why charging slows as the cell approaches full. The reader is an engineer from another field.
trials.a:
A lithium-ion cell is charged with a two-stage protocol called constant-current, constant-voltage (CC-CV). In the first stage the charger forces a fixed current into the cell, commonly expressed as a C-rate, where 1C is the current that would fill the rated capacity in one hour. While this current flows, the cell's terminal voltage rises steadily from roughly 3.0 V toward a ceiling of about 4.2 V for a typical graphite and cobalt-oxide chemistry. When the terminal voltage reaches that ceiling, the charger switches to the second stage. It now holds the voltage fixed and lets the current fall on its own, ending the charge when the current has decayed to a small fraction of the rate, often around 0.05C.

The reason for this shape lies in how the cell stores energy. Charging moves lithium ions from the cathode through the electrolyte and inserts them, or intercalates them, into the graphite anode, while electrons travel through the external circuit. The terminal voltage you measure is not the cell's equilibrium potential. It is the open-circuit voltage, which depends on how much lithium is stored, plus the voltage drop across the cell's internal resistance. That resistance has several parts: ohmic resistance in the electrodes and electrolyte, charge-transfer resistance at the particle surfaces, and a diffusion contribution as ions move through the solid particles and the electrolyte.

During constant current, the resistive drop is roughly steady, so the terminal voltage tracks the slowly climbing open-circuit voltage. Near the end of charge, the open-circuit voltage is already close to its ceiling, and the resistive drop is added on top of it. The terminal voltage therefore hits the limit while the electrode particles are still not fully filled. Lithium concentrates near the particle surfaces, because diffusion into the interior is slow compared with the rate at which ions arrive. Continuing at full current would push the surface potential past safe limits.

The voltage limit exists because the anode would otherwise be driven toward the potential at which lithium plates as metal, forming dendrites that can short the cell, and because a high cathode potential oxidizes the electrolyte and damages the cathode. Holding the voltage constant is the safe way to keep delivering charge. As lithium accumulates, the open-circuit voltage creeps up toward the held value, which shrinks the driving voltage across the internal resistance. By Ohm's law the current must fall in proportion. The decay is roughly exponential, governed by the same diffusion time constants that limit how fast the particle interiors equilibrate.

This is why the final 20 percent of capacity can take as long as the first 80. It is a physical limit on how fast lithium can redistribute inside the electrode particles, not a software choice. Faster charging systems shorten the first stage with higher currents, and temperature control and cell design help, but the taper remains.
trials.b:
Lithium-ion cells are charged with a two-stage protocol called constant-current, constant-voltage (CC-CV). The cell behaves like a nonlinear voltage source with an internal resistance, so the charger controls current and watches terminal voltage.

Stage 1, constant current (CC). The charger forces a fixed current, typically 0.5C to 1C (a 1C current is the one that would fill the rated capacity in an hour). Terminal voltage rises steadily from about 3.0 V toward the cell's upper limit, commonly 4.2 V for graphite/cobalt-oxide chemistries (some newer chemistries use 4.35 V or more, and LFP uses about 3.65 V). During this stage most of the charge goes in, roughly 70 to 80 percent of capacity. Lithium ions leave the cathode, cross the electrolyte and separator, and intercalate (insert between the carbon layers) into the graphite anode.

Stage 2, constant voltage (CV). When terminal voltage reaches the limit, the charger stops forcing current and instead holds voltage fixed. The current then decays roughly exponentially. Charging ends when current falls to a cutoff, typically 0.05C to 0.1C.

Why current must fall. Terminal voltage is the cell's open-circuit voltage (OCV, set by the state of charge) plus the current times the internal resistance, plus polarization terms: V = OCV(SOC) + I·R + overpotentials. Near full, OCV is already close to the limit. Holding V at the limit means the allowed I·R and overpotential budget is shrinking, so current must fall as OCV climbs. This is the same behavior as charging a capacitor through a resistor from a fixed-voltage source, with the cell's OCV acting as the capacitor voltage.

Physical reasons the cell is hard to fill at the end:
1. Solid-state diffusion. Lithium must diffuse into the graphite particles. As the surface fills, the concentration gradient driving diffusion flattens, so the interior fills slowly. The surface looks full to the voltage measurement while the core is not.
2. Electrolyte and electrode transport limits. Ion concentration gradients across the thick porous electrodes build up at high current and relax only gradually.
3. Fewer vacant sites. Intercalation kinetics slow as the available sites vanish.

Why the limit is not raised. Pushing voltage or current harder near full risks lithium plating (metallic lithium deposits on the anode surface instead of intercalating, which causes capacity loss and short-circuit hazard), accelerated electrolyte oxidation and cathode degradation at high voltage, and heat generation. Plating is worst when the anode potential nears 0 V versus lithium, which happens at high current, high state of charge and low temperature.

Practical consequences. The CV stage is slow: the last 20 to 30 percent can take as long as the first 70 to 80 percent. Fast-charging systems therefore taper current in steps, based on temperature, voltage and state of charge, and often stop near 80 percent. Battery management systems also enforce temperature windows (typically no charging below about 0 C) and balance the voltage between series-connected cells.

trials.brief: Write an opinion piece of about 500 words on whether software teams should stop estimating how long work will take. Take a side and argue for it. The readers are working engineers and their managers.
trials.a:
**Stop Estimating. Start Forecasting.**

Every engineer has lived this meeting. Someone asks how long a feature will take. You say three weeks, because two sounds reckless and four sounds lazy. That number gets written down, repeated upward, and turned into a date. Six weeks later you are explaining a miss that was baked in from the start.

Teams should stop producing estimates of how long individual pieces of work will take. Not because planning is bad, but because estimates are bad at the one job we hand them.

Start with the evidence. Software work is dominated by discovery. The tasks we can predict well are the ones we automate or have done a dozen times. What remains is, by construction, the part nobody has done before, and we are asking people to put a number on it. Studies of project overruns keep finding the same thing: errors are large, skewed toward the late side, and resistant to training. Fifteen years of practice makes people more confident, not more accurate.

Worse, the estimate does not stay an estimate. It hardens into a commitment the moment it leaves the room. Managers need to coordinate with sales, support and other teams, so they quote it onward as a date. Engineers learn this and pad. Managers learn that, and trim. Both sides are now negotiating a fiction. The time spent on planning poker, story points and re-estimation is real; the accuracy gained is not.

The honest objection is that the business needs dates. It does. But you can get them without asking anyone to guess at each ticket. Break work into pieces small enough to be roughly comparable, count how many items your team finishes per week, and forecast from that history. If you have shipped eight to fourteen items a week for the last quarter, and there are sixty items left, you can say with real confidence that it lands in roughly five to eight weeks. That range comes from what your team actually did, not from what anyone hoped. A Monte Carlo run over your throughput data takes an afternoon to set up and beats any estimation ritual I have seen.

This approach also changes the conversation in a useful way. Instead of "why did it take longer than you said," the question becomes "is this slice small enough, and is scope growing?" Those are things a team can control. Slicing work thinly forces clarity about what is actually being built. Watching the count of remaining items tells you about scope creep far earlier than a burndown of inflated points.

Some work will not fit. A genuinely novel research spike, a migration with unknown dependencies: for these, timebox the exploration and decide what you will do when the box closes. That is a budget, not an estimate. You are saying how much you are willing to spend, then learning what you can.

Managers, the hard part is yours. You must be willing to hear a range instead of a date, and to treat a missed forecast as new information rather than a failure of character. Engineers, your part is to keep work small and flowing.

Stop asking people to predict the unpredictable. Measure what happened, forecast from it, and spend the saved hours building the thing.
trials.b:
Software teams should stop estimating how long work will take, or at least stop treating estimates as commitments, and the sooner engineers and managers admit this, the better their software will get.

Start with the evidence everyone already knows. Estimates are wrong, and not randomly wrong. They are wrong in one direction, with a long tail of disasters. Fred Brooks wrote about this in the seventies, Hofstadter gave it a law, and every engineer has lived it: the task that was supposed to take three days takes three weeks because of a migration nobody knew existed. We have fifty years of data and the conclusion is the same each time. Software work is discovery, and you cannot schedule discovery.

The standard reply is that estimates are not predictions, they are planning tools. In practice that distinction evaporates the moment a number is written down. A story point becomes a day count in someone's head, the day count becomes a date on a roadmap, and the date becomes a promise made to a customer or an executive. When the work slips, as it will, the team does not hear "our model of the world was incomplete." It hears "you were slow." So engineers learn to pad, managers learn to discount the padding, and both sides spend hours of planning poker negotiating a fiction.

That cost is the part people undercount. Estimation meetings eat real time. Worse, they distort the work. Teams pick the safe, well-understood task over the valuable, uncertain one because the first is easier to size. They cut corners on tests and cleanup to hit a number they never believed. They hide the discovery that the plan was wrong, because bad news is expensive when a date is attached.

Managers worry that without estimates there is no planning. But the alternative is not chaos. It is smaller batches and honest measurement. Break work into pieces small enough that nobody argues about their size, ship them continuously, and watch your actual throughput. If your team merges around eight changes a week, that number, observed rather than guessed, tells you more about next quarter than any sprint-planning spreadsheet. Forecasting from real flow data is cheap, it is usually more accurate than human guessing, and it does not require anyone to pretend.

For decisions about what to build, replace "how long will this take" with "how much are we willing to spend on this." Set an appetite. If a feature is worth two weeks, the team's job is to find a version that fits in two weeks, cutting scope rather than extending the deadline. This flips the incentive. Instead of defending a guess, people negotiate the thing that is actually negotiable.

There are fair exceptions. If you have a hard external deadline, such as a regulatory date or a conference launch, you do need a rough sense of feasibility, and a quick order-of-magnitude judgment (days, weeks, or quarters) is enough. Nobody needs it to the half-day.

So stop the ritual. Slice work small, measure what ships, set budgets instead of predictions, and tell stakeholders the truth: we can tell you what we will have in two weeks, but not what we will have in six months. That honesty is uncomfortable for about a quarter, and then it becomes the best trust-building tool a team has.

trials.brief: Write a narrative account of about 500 words of the Boston molasses flood of 1919. The reader is a general reader.
trials.a:
On a mild January afternoon in 1919, Boston's North End was busy with ordinary life. It was January 15, a few minutes past noon, and the temperature had climbed unexpectedly to about forty degrees after days of bitter cold. Workers ate lunch, children played near the waterfront, and horses and trucks moved along Commercial Street beneath the elevated railway. Looming over it all was a huge steel tank, fifty feet tall and nearly ninety feet across, owned by the United States Industrial Alcohol Company. It held more than two million gallons of molasses, which the company planned to turn into industrial alcohol, a trade that was growing fast as Prohibition approached.

The tank had never been trusted by the neighborhood. Built hastily in 1915, it leaked so badly that residents collected the sticky syrup that ran down its sides. Rather than repair it properly, the company reportedly painted it brown to hide the stains. It was never fully tested, and engineers later found the steel too thin and the rivets poorly set. The tank also groaned and shuddered each time it was filled. Only the day before, a fresh shipment had been pumped in, and the sudden warmth likely made the contents expand and ferment.

Then, with a sound witnesses compared to a machine gun, the rivets began to fail. The tank ruptured and a wave of molasses, perhaps fifteen to twenty-five feet high at its crest, surged out at around thirty-five miles an hour. It carried a force that tore buildings from their foundations. It flattened the nearby firehouse, knocked a freight train's cars off the elevated tracks, and crushed wagons and warehouses beneath it. People were lifted and hurled through the air. Others were pinned in a thick brown current that grew heavier by the second.

The cold made rescue brutally hard. As the molasses cooled, it thickened into something like wet cement, trapping victims where they lay. Sailors from a nearby ship, police, Red Cross workers, and soldiers dug through the mess for survivors, often wading waist-deep. Hospitals filled with the injured. In the end, twenty-one people died, and about a hundred and fifty were hurt. Among the dead were children and a number of city workers who had been eating lunch by the harbor. Horses also perished, and rescuers had a hard time reaching them. The cleanup took weeks, with crews using salt water from fire boats and spreading sand to cover the streets. The harbor ran brown until summer, and locals claimed that on hot days the North End smelled of molasses for decades.

The lawsuit that followed was among the first big class action cases in Massachusetts. The company argued that anarchists had blown up the tank, a claim tied to the fear of radicals at that time. After years of testimony, the court's auditor found that the tank had been unsafe from the start, and the company paid substantial damages to the families. The case helped push changes in American building law, including requirements that engineers sign off on major structures. What began as a freak accident became a lesson in the cost of cutting corners.
trials.b:
On January 15, 1919, a mild winter day in Boston's North End, the city witnessed one of the strangest disasters in American history: a wave of molasses.

At 529 Commercial Street, beside the harbor, stood a huge steel tank owned by the Purity Distilling Company, a subsidiary of United States Industrial Alcohol. It was about fifty feet tall and ninety feet across, and it held roughly 2.3 million gallons of molasses, a raw material used to make industrial alcohol and munitions. The tank had been built quickly in 1915, and it had a troubled life. It leaked so badly that neighbors collected the seeping syrup in pots, and the company reportedly painted the tank brown to hide the stains rather than fix the problem. Workers heard groans from the steel whenever it was filled.

The tank had been filled again just days earlier. Temperatures had been bitterly cold but rose sharply to about 40 degrees Fahrenheit on the fifteenth, which likely thinned the molasses and increased the pressure and fermentation inside.

Shortly after noon, people nearby heard a low rumble, and then a sound some compared to a machine gun as rivets shot out of the tank. The seams burst. A wave of molasses, estimated at fifteen to twenty-five feet high at its crest, surged through the streets at about thirty-five miles per hour.

The force was devastating. The wave tore buildings from their foundations. It buckled the supports of the elevated railway, nearly toppling a train. It crushed a firehouse, where firefighters were trapped in the wreckage. Horses, wagons, and people were swept up and pinned in the thick, sticky flood. Children who had been playing nearby, gathering firewood, were caught in its path.

Rescuers rushed to the scene, including soldiers, sailors from a docked ship, Red Cross workers, and medical teams. They waded through waist-deep molasses, which grew stickier and slower as it cooled in the winter air. Finding survivors was agonizing work. Many victims were trapped, and the molasses clung to everything. In total, twenty-one people died and about 150 were injured.

Cleanup took weeks. Crews sprayed saltwater from fireboats and spread sand to break up the syrup. The harbor ran brown until summer, and people said the neighborhood smelled of molasses for decades afterward.

The aftermath mattered as much as the flood. Hundreds of residents sued the company in one of the first major class action lawsuits in Massachusetts. United States Industrial Alcohol argued that anarchists had bombed the tank, a plausible claim in a postwar period of political unrest. But an auditor, Hugh Ogden, spent years hearing testimony from experts and eyewitnesses, and he concluded that the tank was structurally flawed and the company was responsible, not any bomb. The company ultimately paid settlements to the victims' families, around a million dollars in total.

The disaster helped change how buildings are regulated. It contributed to stronger oversight of construction, including the requirement that engineers review and sign off on plans, and it showed how corporate neglect could carry a deadly cost. Today, a plaque in the North End marks the spot where Boston's sweet, slow catastrophe struck.

trials.brief: Write an explanation of about 600 words of how a heat pump can heat a house when it is colder outside than inside. The reader is a homeowner deciding whether to replace a gas boiler.
trials.a:
A heat pump does not make heat by burning anything. It moves heat that already exists outside and carries it indoors. That is why it works when the air outside is colder than your living room.

**Cold is not zero heat**

Heat is the energy of moving molecules. Air at 0°C still holds a great deal of it. Heat only stops being available at absolute zero, about -273°C. Heat flows naturally from warm to cold, so a cold outdoor coil can absorb heat from the outside air, provided the coil is colder still.

**The refrigeration cycle**

A heat pump is a fridge run in reverse. A sealed loop carries a refrigerant, a fluid that boils at very low temperatures. The loop has four main parts.

1. **Evaporator (outdoor unit).** The refrigerant is kept at very low pressure, so it boils at around -20°C or lower. Outdoor air at, say, 2°C is warmer than that, so heat flows from the air into the refrigerant, which evaporates into a gas.
2. **Compressor.** This electric pump squeezes the gas. Compressing a gas heats it, so the refrigerant leaves at perhaps 50 to 70°C. This is where most of the electricity is used.
3. **Condenser (indoor side).** The hot gas passes its heat to your radiators, underfloor heating, or hot water cylinder. As it gives up heat, it condenses back into a liquid.
4. **Expansion valve.** The liquid is suddenly released into a low-pressure space. Its pressure and temperature drop sharply, and the cycle starts again.

The trick is that pressure sets the boiling point. By changing pressure, the machine makes the refrigerant colder than outside in one place and hotter than your radiators in another.

**Why it beats a gas boiler on efficiency**

A modern gas boiler converts about 90 to 95 percent of its fuel into heat. It cannot do better than 100 percent. A heat pump delivers more heat than the electricity it uses, because most of the output is heat it has moved, not made. This is measured as the coefficient of performance (COP). A COP of 3 means 3 kWh of heat for every 1 kWh of electricity. Over a whole year, typical home systems average a seasonal COP of roughly 2.5 to 4.

**The catch: colder weather lowers efficiency**

The colder it gets outside, the harder the compressor has to work to lift heat up to the temperature you need. COP falls on very cold days, perhaps to 2 or a little lower. Modern units still run in sub-zero conditions, and many are rated down to -15°C or below, but they use more electricity per unit of heat delivered. Defrost cycles are also needed when frost builds on the outdoor coil.

**What this means for your decision**

- **Running cost.** Electricity usually costs more per kWh than gas. A COP of 3 can offset that, but the saving depends on local prices. Check the ratio of your electricity price to your gas price. Roughly, if electricity costs less than three times as much as gas, a heat pump tends to be cheaper to run. Time-of-use tariffs can help further.
- **Your house matters most.** Heat pumps work best at lower flow temperatures (35 to 50°C), compared with 60 to 80°C for many boilers. A well-insulated home with large radiators or underfloor heating suits them. A draughty, poorly insulated house may need insulation upgrades or bigger radiators first. Ask for a proper heat-loss survey, not a rule-of-thumb quote.
- **Upfront cost.** Installation typically costs several times more than a new gas boiler, though grants or subsidies may cover part of it. Ask installers about what is available where you live.
- **Carbon.** Even on a mixed-fuel grid, a heat pump normally produces far less carbon per unit of heat than burning gas, and the gap widens as grids decarbonise.
- **Practicalities.** You need outdoor space for the unit, and usually a hot water cylinder. Noise is modest but worth checking against neighbours' windows.

**A sensible way to decide**

Get at least two quotes that include a heat-loss calculation and a predicted seasonal COP. Ask for estimated annual running costs compared with your current gas bill. If your boiler is near the end of its life, that is the natural moment to switch, since you avoid paying for a new boiler you would soon replace. If it is young and your home is poorly insulated, improving insulation first and revisiting in a few years may be wiser.

In short, a heat pump works in the cold because outdoor air still contains heat, and a pressure-driven refrigerant loop can pull it indoors. Whether it suits you depends on your insulation, your heat emitters, and your energy prices.
trials.b:
A heat pump does not make heat by burning anything. It moves heat that already exists from one place to another, and that is why it can warm your house even when the air outside is colder than the air inside. The trick is that "cold" is relative. Outdoor air at minus five degrees Celsius still holds a great deal of thermal energy, because the energy only vanishes at absolute zero, which is about minus 273 degrees. A heat pump extracts some of that energy and delivers it indoors.

The mechanism is the same one inside your fridge, run in the opposite direction. A sealed loop contains a refrigerant, a fluid chosen because it boils at a very low temperature, far below freezing. Outside, a fan blows air across a coil holding this refrigerant. Because the refrigerant is colder than the air, even on a frosty day, heat flows into it and it evaporates into a gas. Heat always flows from warmer to cooler, so this step works as long as the refrigerant is colder than the outdoor air.

The gas then passes through a compressor, which is the part that uses electricity. Squeezing a gas raises its pressure and, with it, its temperature, so the refrigerant leaves the compressor hotter than your radiators or underfloor heating need, typically well above 40 degrees. Now the direction of flow works in your favour. The hot gas travels through a second coil inside the house, where it gives up its heat to your heating water or indoor air and condenses back into a liquid. An expansion valve then drops the pressure, the refrigerant turns cold again, and the cycle repeats.

The key point for your decision is efficiency. A gas boiler turns each unit of gas energy into at most about 0.9 to 0.95 units of heat. A heat pump uses electricity only to run the compressor and fans, while the bulk of the heat is collected from outdoors. Typically it delivers three to four units of heat for every unit of electricity, a ratio called the coefficient of performance. In very cold weather the ratio falls, perhaps to two or a little more, because the compressor must lift the heat across a bigger temperature gap. Even then it comfortably beats a boiler on energy delivered, though whether it beats it on running cost depends on the price of electricity relative to gas in your area.

There are practical matters to weigh. Heat pumps deliver water at lower temperatures than a boiler, so they work best with large radiators, underfloor heating, or a well-insulated house, since gentle, steady heat is their strength. If your home is draughty or poorly insulated, or your radiators are small, you may need insulation upgrades or some radiator replacements to stay comfortable on the coldest days. Modern units are rated to keep working at minus 15 or even minus 25 degrees, so cold climates are not the barrier they once were, although the outdoor unit may periodically defrost itself, which is normal.

Upfront cost is the main hurdle. Installation usually costs considerably more than a new boiler, though government grants or incentives in many regions narrow the gap. Savings come over years through lower running costs and, if your electricity is increasingly low-carbon, much lower emissions. Ask installers for a heat loss survey of your specific house, a realistic estimate of seasonal efficiency, and a clear list of any extra work needed. If your boiler is near the end of its life and your home is reasonably insulated, a heat pump is often a sound replacement.

trials.brief: Write a narrative account of about 800 words of John Snow's investigation of the 1854 cholera outbreak around Broad Street in London. The reader is a general reader with no medical background.
trials.a:
In late August 1854, a terrible illness arrived in Soho, a crowded, working-class district of London. The illness was cholera, and it killed with frightening speed. A person could be well in the morning, doubled over with violent vomiting and diarrhoea by noon, and dead within a day or two, drained of so much fluid that the skin turned blue and shrivelled. Within about ten days of the outbreak's start, more than five hundred people living within a few streets of one another had died. Many families fled. Shops closed. The neighbourhood around Broad Street, today called Broadwick Street, became a place of mourning and fear.

At the time, almost nobody knew what caused cholera. The dominant belief among doctors and officials was the miasma theory, which held that disease spread through foul-smelling air rising from rotting waste, sewers and swamps. It was a reasonable guess for a city whose streets stank, but it was wrong. Microbes had not yet been accepted as a cause of illness, and the bacterium behind cholera would not be identified in any lasting way for decades.

John Snow, a physician living a short walk from Broad Street, had been thinking about cholera for years. He was an unusual man for his profession: a teetotaller and vegetarian, the son of a labourer, and a pioneer in the use of anaesthetics, having given chloroform to Queen Victoria during childbirth. During an earlier cholera epidemic in 1848 and 1849, he had come to doubt the miasma theory. Cholera, he noted, attacked the bowels first, not the lungs, which is odd if the cause were something breathed in. He suspected instead that people swallowed a poison from contaminated water or food, and that the sick passed it along through their waste. He had published this idea in 1849, but few were persuaded.

When the Soho outbreak began, Snow saw a chance to test his theory. He did not simply argue; he went door to door. He gathered the names and addresses of the dead from the official register of deaths and then visited homes to ask where people had got their drinking water. In that era, there were no taps in most houses. People fetched water from shared street pumps, and different pumps drew from different sources. Snow's questioning soon revealed a pattern. Most of the dead had lived close to the pump on Broad Street, and most of them had drunk its water.

He also noticed the exceptions, which proved more revealing than the rule. A workhouse nearby, home to some five hundred residents, suffered few deaths. Snow learned that it had its own well. A brewery on the same street had no cases among its workers, who were given free beer and, it seems, drank little else; the brewery also had its own supply. On the other hand, a woman who lived far from Soho had died of cholera after her family sent for bottles of water from the Broad Street pump, which she had liked the taste of. Her niece, who also drank it, fell ill too. Each of these cases pointed to the same culprit.

Snow also produced a map. He marked each death with a small black bar at the address where it occurred, and the bars piled up thickly around the Broad Street pump. Maps of this kind were not entirely new, but his was a persuasive picture of the facts, showing that the disease clustered around one particular water source rather than being scattered across the district as bad air might suggest.

On 7 September, Snow took his findings to the local board of guardians, the officials responsible for the parish. He urged them to remove the handle from the Broad Street pump so that no one could draw water from it. The guardians, though sceptical of his theory, agreed to try. The handle came off the next day. The outbreak was by then already declining, as many residents had fled and others had perhaps changed their habits, so the removal cannot be credited with ending it single-handedly. Still, the gesture became famous.

Snow was not finished. Later investigation uncovered the likely source of contamination. A local clergyman, Henry Whitehead, who had initially doubted Snow's ideas, carried out his own careful inquiries and found that the first known victim, a baby girl, had fallen ill shortly before the outbreak. Her mother had washed the child's soiled nappies and emptied the water into a cesspit very close to the Broad Street well. When the pit was examined, its brickwork was found to be decayed, and it was leaking into the ground near the well. Whitehead eventually became one of Snow's strongest supporters.

Official authorities were less convinced. An inquiry concluded that the evidence did not establish Snow's claim, and the miasma theory remained influential for years. Snow died in 1858, aged only forty-five, without seeing his ideas widely accepted. Yet in time, as the germ theory of disease took hold and the cholera bacterium was firmly linked to contaminated water, his work was recognised as a milestone. Today he is remembered as a founder of modern epidemiology, the study of how diseases spread through populations, and the Broad Street pump is marked by a replica in the street where it once stood.
trials.b:
In late August 1854, cholera struck Soho, a crowded district of London. Within ten days, more than five hundred people living within a few hundred yards of one another had died. Cholera is a disease of violent diarrhoea and dehydration that can kill a healthy adult in a day. In 1854 nobody knew what caused it.

Most educated people, including most doctors, believed in miasma. This was the idea that disease spread through foul air rising from rotting waste, filthy streets and sewers. The theory seemed sensible in a city that stank. London was full of cesspools, overflowing drains and a river that carried its own sewage past the city.

John Snow, a physician who lived and worked in Soho, did not accept this. Snow was a quiet, teetotal man best known for pioneering the use of anaesthesia. He had given chloroform to Queen Victoria during childbirth. He had also studied cholera in the epidemic of 1848-49 and reached an unfashionable conclusion. Cholera, he argued, attacked the bowels first, not the lungs, so it must be swallowed, not breathed in. Something in contaminated water or food, passed from the sick to the healthy, was the likelier culprit. Few people took him seriously.

When the 1854 outbreak erupted almost on his doorstep, Snow went to work. He did not start with a theory about the air. He started with the dead. He obtained the death records from the local registrar and found where each victim had lived. Then he walked the streets and knocked on doors, asking families where they had got their water.

At that time, most Londoners had no water pipes in their homes. They drew water from public pumps, which were fed from wells dug into the ground or from water companies that piped in supplies from the Thames. The pump at the corner of Broad Street and Cambridge Street was popular. Its water was cool and clear, and people thought it tasted sweet.

Snow marked each death on a map of the district. The deaths clustered thickly around the Broad Street pump, and the pattern became clearer the more closely he examined it. Almost everyone who had died lived closer to that pump than to any other. Some of the exceptions taught him even more.

Near the pump stood a workhouse housing more than five hundred people. Only five of them died. Snow learned that the workhouse had its own well and so did not rely on the Broad Street pump. A brewery on Broad Street employed seventy workers, and none of them died of cholera. The men were given free beer, and the brewery had its own well. There was also a woman who lived far from Soho, in Hampstead, and who died of cholera. Snow discovered that she had once lived in Broad Street and so liked the taste of the water that she had it carried to her house every day. A niece who drank the same water died too.

By the evening of 7 September, Snow was convinced. He went to the board of guardians of St James's parish, the local authority, and presented his evidence. They were sceptical, but they agreed to act. On the following day, the handle was removed from the pump, so that it could not be used. New cases fell sharply soon afterwards.

The story is often told as if the removal of the handle ended the epidemic, but the truth is less tidy. The outbreak had already been declining, partly because many residents had fled the district. Snow himself admitted that the fall in cases might have happened anyway. The handle was a sign of his conviction, not a decisive experiment.

The map's real value was its power to persuade. Snow did not stop there. He and the Reverend Henry Whitehead, a local curate who started out as a sceptic, kept investigating. Whitehead interviewed residents and traced the first case to a baby girl who had fallen ill with diarrhoea just before the outbreak. Her mother had washed the baby's soiled nappies and thrown the water into a cesspool, which lay only a few feet from the Broad Street well. When the well was examined, the brickwork was found to be cracked, allowing sewage to seep in.

Snow also carried out a larger study during the same epidemic. He compared households in south London supplied by two water companies. One drew its water from a part of the Thames contaminated with the city's sewage. The other had moved its intake upriver, to a cleaner stretch. Households served by the first company suffered far more deaths. People on the same streets, living in similar conditions, had very different fates depending only on their water.

Even so, official bodies rejected his conclusions. A committee investigating the outbreak found no proof that the pump was to blame, and miasma remained the accepted view. Snow died in 1858, aged forty-five, still largely unconvinced of his own vindication in the eyes of his peers. It was not until the 1880s, when Robert Koch identified the cholera bacterium, that his work was fully accepted.

Today Snow is remembered as a founder of modern epidemiology, the study of how disease spreads through populations. His method was simple. He counted, mapped, compared and asked questions, and he followed the evidence even where it led against received opinion.
